title: The Clock Comes to Dinner

pages.text:
I opened the door before he could knock again. Jonah Park stood on the step, his bike helmet strapped under his chin. He held up a folder that was laminated so thick it looked like armor.

"The Last Day Extravaganza," he announced, his voice cracking with excitement. "Item one: Weller Creek. Bring water shoes. Item two: Putt-Putt Palace. I have already studied the hole numbers. Item three: Scoops. We order the double scoop chocolate with the cherry on top. No exceptions."

He read it with the seriousness of a lawyer presenting a case. I leaned against the doorframe, crossing my arms over my red hoodie.

"I might come," I said.

His grin, which had been wide enough to show both rows of teeth, wobbled. Just for half a second. Then he fixed it back in place, rigid and bright.

"Two o'clock," he said. "Wet shoes."

He spun around on one heel and pedaled away, his helmet bobbing against the sun. I closed the door and listened to the tires hiss on the asphalt until they were gone. The silence that remained felt heavy, like a wool blanket thrown over a chair.
pages.image: Jonah, an 11-year-old boy with a buzz cut and huge grin, stands on a porch step wearing a bike helmet, holding a thick laminated folder; Max in a red hoodie leans in the doorway looking bored; suburban street background.

pages.text:
Lunch at 12:30 was peanut butter sandwiches on paper towels. The plates were packed, so we ate standing up in the empty kitchen, which smelled like cardboard and dust.

Dad held up a slice of bread. "You know why bread is better than toast?"

"Because it doesn't burn?" I offered.

"No, Max. Because it's soft. It's like a hug for your mouth."

Nobody laughed. Mom stood by the counter, her pencil tapping against page four of her checklist. Tessa was not there. I knew she was upstairs because I could hear the faint, rhythmic thump-thump of her drumsticks tapping against the wall.

Gus sat on the floor, holding his sandwich with both hands. He looked at it, then at me. He let out a low, rumbling growl.

"Raaawr," he said softly.

He bit into the bread. The peanut butter smeared on his green T. rex sleeve. I watched him eat, and I noticed that nobody else was really eating. We were just chewing, waiting for the taste of the day to fade, hoping it would turn into something we could swallow without choking.
pages.image: A family eats peanut butter sandwiches on paper towels in a bare kitchen; Dad in a fish apron smiles, Mom holds a clipboard, a small boy in a green T. rex costume sits on the floor holding his sandwich; boxes stack in the background.

pages.text:
At 1:15, a horn played a tune. It was not the normal honk. It was a melody, three notes high and one low, like a trumpet clearing its throat.

The green Buick rolled into the driveway. It was enormous, the color of a forest after rain. The door opened, and out stepped Grandma Bea. She was tiny, wearing huge round sunglasses and a coat that was bright red. Gold bangles on her wrists jingled with every step.

In her hands, she carried a laundry basket. Inside the basket, wrapped in a dish towel, was a wooden clock.

"Max," she said, her voice warm and sharp. "I decided you are keeping this."

"I don't want a clock, Nonna," I said. "I want to stay."

She stopped. She looked at me over the top of her sunglasses. Her eyes were dark and serious behind the glass.

"Nobody asked what you want, caro," she said. "I am asking what you will do."
pages.image: Grandma Bea, a tiny woman in red lipstick and large round sunglasses, steps out of a large green car in a driveway holding a laundry basket containing a wooden clock; Max in a red hoodie stands on the porch looking upset.

pages.text:
She hung the clock on the last hook in the front hall. It was a tall, dark wood cabinet with a small door.

"Meet Gerald," she said.

Gerald was a painted wooden bird. He had a crooked beak and eyebrows that looked permanently angry. It was the quarter hour. The small door creaked open. Gerald popped out.

"Cuck-oo," he said. It was not a happy sound. It was a fussy, complaining sound.

Gus, who had been hiding behind Grandma Bea's leg, roared. "RAAAAWR!"

Gerald vanished back into the door.

"See?" Grandma Bea said, jingling her bangles. "He has opinions."

"Clocks don't have opinions," I said. "They have mechanisms."

Ten seconds later, the door creaked open again. Gerald poked his head out, looked at me, and gave one loud, angry cuckoo before hiding again. I stared at the wooden bird. He stared back, or at least, his painted eyes seemed to.
pages.image: A small wooden cuckoo clock hangs on a hook in a hallway; a painted wooden bird with angry eyebrows pops out of the door; Gus in a T. rex costume roars at it; Grandma Bea watches with a smile.

pages.text:
It was 2:00. The Extravaganza had started without me.

I climbed out my window and onto the garage roof. It was dusty, but it was mine, and it was high enough to see the whole street. I pulled a bag of pretzels from my pocket.

Jonah’s bike came down the street. He was pedaling hard, his helmet bobbing. He looked up, then down the empty street. His shoulders slumped. He looked like a person who had lost a game he didn’t know they were playing.

He pedaled on. The laminated itinerary flapped in the wind behind him, a white flag of hope.

I ate a pretzel. It tasted like nothing. Not salty, not sweet, just dry air and salt. I told myself I didn’t care. I am going to be honest with you for the rest of this book, so: I lied.
pages.image: Max in a red hoodie sits on a dusty garage roof holding a bag of pretzels; below, Jonah in a bike helmet rides a bike down the street, looking lonely; a suburban neighborhood with green lawns and houses.
